crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Drafting a Manuscript
children.blurb: Drafting a manuscript is the work of turning research findings into a structured document that can be submitted to a journal or conference.

children.name: Testing Arguments Before Peer Review
children.blurb: Testing arguments before peer review covers the work a researcher does to stress-test a paper's claims, reasoning, evidence, and framing before submitting it to a journal or conference.

children.name: Disciplinary Register and Language
children.blurb: Disciplinary register and language in academic writing and peer review covers how fields such as machine learning, cognitive science, linguistics, and medicine use distinct vocabulary, sentence patterns, citation habits, and levels of formality.

children.name: Plagiarism and AI Detection
children.blurb: Plagiarism and AI detection covers the identification of copied text, unattributed ideas, and machine generated content in academic writing and peer review.

children.name: Explaining Research After Publication
children.blurb: Explaining research after publication covers the work of translating a peer-reviewed or preprint paper into forms that non-specialists, practitioners, journalists, and other researchers can use.

sections.body: Academic writing and peer review is the part of research practice where a finding becomes a claim that other people can read, check and cite. Artificial intelligence now sits at several points in that chain. It drafts and restructures sections of manuscripts, proposes counterarguments a reviewer might raise, checks whether a passage matches existing literature, and helps translate dense results into summaries for wider audiences. Journals and conferences have responded with disclosure rules and detection tools, so the technology is as much a subject of policy as a writing aid. The work here is practical: getting a paper into a form that survives scrutiny.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Language generation is genuinely useful for turning notes into readable prose and for flagging gaps in an argument before submission. Detection of AI written text remains unreliable, with false positives falling hardest on non native English writers, and no detector output should be treated as proof of misconduct. Originality checking against published work is more mature, though it depends on the databases it can reach. What is not solved is authorship, because responsibility for a claim still rests with the named human authors, and no tool can verify that a cited source says what the manuscript claims it says. The honest limit is that these systems assist judgement rather than replace it.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The section moves in the order a paper actually travels. Drafting a Manuscript covers turning results into a structured document, and Testing Arguments Before Peer Review is where you stress the reasoning against the objections a referee is likely to make. Disciplinary Register and Language deals with writing that sounds native to a field, which matters most for authors working outside their first language. Plagiarism and AI Detection sits at the compliance boundary, explaining what these tools can and cannot establish. Explaining Research After Publication closes the loop, taking a finished paper to readers beyond the original audience. Read together they trace one manuscript from first draft to public reach.
